content: Acer, commonly referred to as maple, is a genus of trees or shrubs. These plants are classified either in their own family, Aceraceae, or within the family Sapindaceae, which also includes the Hippocastanaceae. Modern botanical classification systems, such as the Angiosperm Phylogeny Group system, generally place maples within the Sapindaceae family. The type species of this genus is Acer pseudoplatanus, also known as the Sycamore maple. There are approximately 128 recognized species of maples. The majority of these species are native to Asia, although several species are also found in Europe, northern Africa, and North America. Only one species, Acer laurinum, is native to the Southern Hemisphere, and it has not been extensively studied. Alarmingly, 54 species of maples are classified as threatened with extinction in their natural habitats, according to the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN). The name Acer is derived from the Latin word meaning sharp, which is a reference to the pointed shape of maple leaves. This name was first assigned to the genus by the French botanist Joseph Pitton de Tournefort in the year 1700. The earliest known fossil evidence of a maple species is Acer alaskense, which dates back to the Latest Paleocene epoch and was discovered in Alaska.
